findings.title: The neighbor-query interface is per-agent only, contradicting the vectorized hot-loop requirement and this doc's own success criterion
findings.description:
`query_radius(position, radius)` accepts a single position, and data-flow step 3 (`:88`) says "For each *active* agent" — i.e. one Python-level call per active agent per tick, returning a ragged variable-length array. That is the dominant tick cost per the architecture ("neighbor finding typically dominates tick cost", `100-arch.behavior-engine.md:87`), which also requires the hot loop to be "structured for vectorized computation over arrays of agent state, not object-by-object iteration" (`:33`) and the force interface to stay GPU-compatible with "no Python-level per-agent branching, no dynamic allocation, and no callbacks into Python during the hot loop" (`:99`). The slice's own technical requirement at `:247` ("No Python-level per-agent loops in the hot path") is unachievable for neighbor gathering as specified — it is silently narrowed to force accumulation and integration only.

This matters beyond style because the doc declares the protocol final for consumers: `:224` states slice 105 "provides an optimized implementation" behind this interface, and the slice plan says 105 swaps the strategy "behind the existing query interface" with identical output (`100-slices.behavior-engine.md:26`). A spatial hash cannot remove the per-agent Python loop or the ragged `neighbor_lists` hand-off, so 105 will either have to extend the protocol or leave the hot loop per-agent. Add a bulk query method now (e.g. `query_radius_bulk(positions, radii) -> (indices, offsets)` in CSR/padded form) and make it the path `tick()` uses, or state explicitly that the protocol is expected to gain a bulk method in 105 and that 105's "identical output" regression is against the per-agent method.

findings.title: Two force protocols are defined but only one is consumed, and the dispatch rule is self-contradictory
findings.description:
`tick()` takes `forces: list[BulkForce]` (`:185`), so nothing in this slice calls the per-agent `Force` protocol. Yet `:152` says "The tick loop prefers the bulk variant when available", which implies a mixed list and a per-call capability check the signature does not permit, and success criterion `:248` requires placeholder forces to "exercise both the `Force` and `BulkForce` protocol paths" — a path exercised only by a test, never by the engine. A per-agent force path in the hot loop is precisely what `100-arch.behavior-engine.md:99` rules out.

Cut the per-agent `Force` protocol (and its `ConstantDriftSingle` placeholder, tasks §6.2/§6.3) from this slice, or, if it is genuinely wanted as a reference/testing seam, say so explicitly: it is a test-only adapter, it is never accepted by `tick()`, and delete the "prefers the bulk variant when available" sentence. As written, slices 101–104 cannot tell which protocol they are supposed to implement.

findings.title: `BulkForce` parameter semantics are under-specified for the four slices that must implement it
findings.description:
`BulkForce` is the interface 101–104 conform to (`:223`), but three things a consumer needs are unstated:
- `neighbor_lists: list[NDArray[np.intp]]` — is it aligned to `active_indices` order or to full-population index order? What is the entry for an inactive agent (`None`, empty array)? Is it ragged or padded/CSR?
- `profiles: list[BehavioralProfile]` — the profile registry indexed by `state.profile_indices` (as `tick()`'s own docstring at `:192` describes), or a per-agent expansion parallel to `neighbor_lists`? The two readings produce different implementations.
- Whether the force array returned must be zero-initialized for inactive agents by the implementation or whether `tick()` zeroes it (relevant once several forces are summed).

Also, `list[NDArray]` is a ragged Python container, which weakens the doc's claim that this is the "future GPU boundary" (`:139`) against `100-arch.behavior-engine.md:99` ("bulk array-in/array-out"). Pin the ordering convention, the inactive-agent representation, and whether neighbor data is padded or offset-based before 101 starts; this is the cheapest moment to fix it.

findings.title: No NFR target restated for the tick/spatial path this slice creates
findings.description:
The slice builds the two paths carrying the architecture's stated NFRs: "tens of thousands of agents at full behavioral fidelity on a single CPU process" (`100-arch.behavior-engine.md:33`) and a tick rate "slow enough that the server can complete a full tick within the budget" (`:93`). The Technical Requirements list has no performance item at all — only "no Python-level per-agent loops". The single scale statement in the doc is qualitative and about the reference implementation: "acceptable for the hundreds-of-agents scale this slice targets" (`:173`).

Two concrete gaps follow. First, `BruteForceQuery.build()` stores the full N×N pairwise-distance matrix every tick (`:173`), which is ~800 MB of float64 at the architecture's 10K-agent target; the doc sets no agent-count ceiling and no guard, so the failure is an out-of-memory crash discovered at runtime rather than a documented limit. Second, with no per-tick target, "don't optimize in this slice" (`:309`) has no measurable boundary. Restate the NFR with the numbers this slice is accountable for — e.g. "N ≤ 1,000 agents, full tick (build + query + forces + integrate) ≤ X ms at dt=1/60; the O(n²) build is bounded by that N and is replaced in 105" — and state the memory consequence of the N×N matrix explicitly. Note that `200-arch.world-server-foundation.md`, which the parent docs cite for scaling tiers and tick budget, is not present in `project-documents/user/architecture/`, so no numeric budget exists upstream to inherit; this slice has to state its own.

findings.title: The architecture's "Environment as input surface" principle has no entry point, yet `tick()` is declared final for later slices
findings.description:
The word "environment" does not appear in the slice design. The architecture lists environmental queries as one of the three interfaces the engine exposes under "Clean boundaries" (`100-arch.behavior-engine.md:35`) and devotes a principle to it: the engine "queries environmental state (terrain elevation, resource locations, threat zones, seasonal parameters) through a read-only interface" (`:47`). Meanwhile this doc promises consumers that `tick()` is "the integration loop that slices use as-is. Behavioral slices add forces; they don't modify the tick loop" (`:225`).

Those two statements cannot both hold unless the environment entry path is named. It is defensible to defer the interface itself (no slice in the plan before 106/107 needs it, and 104's home-range center can live in `AgentState`), but the deferral should be explicit and should say *how* environment will arrive — e.g. forces are constructed as closures over an environment handle supplied by the caller, so `tick()` never gains an environment parameter — because that choice is what keeps `:225` true. Add it to Excluded with the mechanism, or drop the "used as-is / don't modify the tick loop" claim.

findings.title: Failure modes for index inputs are unspecified, and the fancy-indexing accumulation described is wrong for duplicate indices
findings.description:
`state.velocities[active_indices] += ...` does not accumulate for repeated indices — NumPy buffers the read and writes once — so a caller passing duplicates (a plausible world-server bug when merging per-region active sets) silently loses force contributions instead of failing. Negative indices silently wrap; out-of-range indices raise a bare `IndexError` from deep inside integration with no context. The same is true of `state.profile_indices` values that exceed `len(profiles)`, which the design relies on for per-agent `query_radius` and `max_speed` (`:88`, `:213`) but never validates.

CLAUDE.md forbids silent fallbacks and requires failing explicitly, and the architecture requires the force/spatial interfaces to "function correctly when only a subset of the population is being evaluated" (`100-arch.behavior-engine.md:97`) — correctness of the subset path is this slice's headline deliverable. Specify the contract: duplicate/negative/out-of-range `active_indices` raise a validation error (or are documented as caller-undefined and asserted in debug), out-of-range `profile_indices` raise rather than index garbage, and use an accumulation form that is correct for the chosen contract (`np.add.at` if duplicates are legal). The n=0 and empty-`active_indices` cases should also be named; tasks §3.3 covers n=0 for state but nothing covers an empty subset in `tick()`.

findings.title: `accelerations` is dead state and the force→acceleration semantics (unit mass) are never stated
findings.description:
`accelerations` (N×2 float64) is listed in scope (`:35`) and in the `AgentState` contents (`:96`), but nothing in the design reads or writes it: integration is `velocity += force * dt` (`:207-211`), the tick data flow never mentions it (`:89-92`), and the integrator described in tasks §4.1 takes positions, velocities, forces, dt, max_speeds — no accelerations. It is allocated-and-forgotten state, which CLAUDE.md's "resist adding complexity" argues against; cut it, or say which step populates it.

The deeper issue it hides: `force * dt` added to velocity treats the force array as an acceleration, i.e. unit mass for every agent. That assumption is never stated, and `BehavioralProfile` has no mass field (`:237`, `:299`). Slices 101–104 will be writing cohesion/pursuit/flight "forces" against this contract, and predator-prey in particular is where a mass difference would naturally be wanted. State the convention explicitly ("force arrays are accelerations; mass is 1.0 and is not a profile parameter in this slice") so later slices do not discover it mid-implementation.

findings.title: The Integration section is indented four spaces and renders as a code block, not a heading
findings.description: `### Integration: Semi-Implicit Euler` and its three following paragraphs are indented, so in rendered markdown they become part of the preceding code block under "Tick Function Signature" instead of a sibling `###` heading. The content (semi-implicit Euler, `max_speed` clamp source, subset integration) is correct and matches `100-arch.behavior-engine.md:93`; only the indentation needs removing so the section is navigable.

findings.title: Overview says the tick returns updated state; the design mutates in place and returns None
findings.description: Included-scope bullet: "integrate (semi-implicit Euler), return updated state", versus `def tick(...) -> None` with "state: Agent state arrays, mutated in place" (`:177-192`) and data-flow step 6 "mutated in place" (`:92`). In-place mutation is the right call and is consistent with the architecture's "engine is stateless between ticks" (`100-arch.behavior-engine.md:69`), even though the architecture's step 5 says "Returns the updated state array" (`:68`) — the deviation is an improvement, not a violation. Just fix `:39` so the deliverable's contract is stated once, unambiguously; a consumer reading only the scope list would write `state = tick(...)`.

findings.title: `DIMS`-based 3D parameterization is speculative scope
findings.description: No slice in the plan, and nothing in the architecture or concept, calls for 3D simulation state — the 3D work in the concept is client-side rendering and terrain mesh. The `DIMS = 2` constant plus shape assertions keyed to it (tasks §1.1, §3.3) is small, but it is abstraction nothing uses yet, and the "single-point change" claim is optimistic: force math, the spatial query, and the profile's radius/speed semantics would all need review regardless. Keeping it is defensible as a one-line constant; if anything in this slice is trimmed for effort, this and the per-agent `Force` protocol are the first candidates.
